**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Senior Partner
**FROM:** [Your Name]
**DATE:** October 26, 2023
**RE:** Duty of Care Owed by Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation Regarding Service Estimates in *Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. v. Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation*, No. G-24-115-AA

---

## Executive Summary
Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation (“Gulfstream”) likely owed a professional duty of reasonable care in preparing and communicating its service estimates to Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. (“CITIOM”). While Gulfstream contractually disclaimed liability for estimates related to unforeseen discrepancies, this limitation may be unenforceable under Georgia law if CITIOM can demonstrate that Gulfstream's preparation of the initial estimate constituted gross negligence, as an expert witness has alleged.

## Factual Background
This dispute arises from a 192-month inspection of a Gulfstream G550 aircraft, Serial Number 5174 (“the Aircraft”), owned by CITIOM. Gulfstream, which had previously performed a 144-month inspection on the same Aircraft, provided a "192-Month Inspection Proposal" quoting an estimated 2,800 manhours and a downtime of 35-45 business days. [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]]. The proposal explicitly stated that the estimate did not include time or cost for correcting discrepancies that might be discovered during the inspection. [Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief .pdf, p. 2 [VERIFIED]].

CITIOM alleges that it agreed to the proposal in reliance on Gulfstream’s express representations and expertise. [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]]. Upon commencement of the work, the project’s scope expanded dramatically to over 26,000 labor hours, nearly ten times the initial estimate. [Danny Farnham Direct Outline with Cross & Redirect.docx, p. 1 [UNVERIFIED]]. This was attributed to extensive corrosion in previously worked-on areas and other discovered discrepancies. [In re CITCOM v Gulfstream - Analysis of Claims and Defenses Related to Repairs on GS550-5174(80915932.pdf, p. 1 [UNVERIFIED]]. The project was also beset by mismanagement, including the reassignment of experienced technicians and significant delays and aesthetic defects in paint work performed under the supervision of Patrick Stockton. [6. Patrick Stockton - Cross Exam & Impeachment.docx, p. 1 [UNVERIFIED]].

CITIOM has proffered an expert, D. Farnham, who opines that Gulfstream was “grossly negligent” for failing to include a reasonable estimation for discrepancy-related costs and for not utilizing its own “newly available data analytics” capabilities, which were introduced in July 2023, prior to the proposal. [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 5 [UNVERIFIED]; CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]]. CITIOM has subsequently initiated arbitration proceedings against Gulfstream.

## Analysis

### Key Findings
- **Significant Disparity in Estimates:** Gulfstream’s initial estimate of 2,800 manhours was grossly disproportionate to the more than 26,000 labor hours ultimately required to complete the inspection and repairs. [Danny Farnham Direct Outline with Cross & Redirect.docx, p. 1 [UNVERIFIED]; CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]].
- **Client Reliance:** CITIOM expressly relied upon Gulfstream's proposal, believing it to be accurate, when it decided to input the Aircraft for service at Gulfstream's St. Louis facility. [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]].
- **Contractual Limitation:** Gulfstream’s proposal contained explicit language stating that its estimates for cost and downtime did not account for the correction of discrepancies found during the inspection. [Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief .pdf, p. 2 [VERIFIED]].
- **Expert Allegation of Gross Negligence:** CITIOM's expert, D. Farnham, alleges that Gulfstream's proposal process was "grossly negligent" and "blatantly negligent" for its failure to include any contingency for discrepancy-related work and for its failure to leverage available data analytics to provide a more realistic projection. [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 5 [UNVERIFIED]].
- **Governing Law on Liability Limitations:** Under Georgia law, while exculpatory clauses relieving a party from its own ordinary negligence are generally valid, clauses that purport to relieve liability for acts of gross negligence or willful or wanton conduct are void as against public policy. [In re CITCOM v Gulfstream - Analysis of Claims and Defenses Related to Repairs on GS550-5174(80915932.pdf, p. 4 [UNVERIFIED]].
- **Failure to Utilize Available Technology:** Gulfstream possessed "new data collection and analytical capabilities" designed to set "reasonable expectations" for operators before CITIOM’s aircraft was inducted, but it did not use these capabilities to inform or update the estimate provided. [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]].

### Supporting Evidence
The strongest evidence supporting a breach of a duty of care stems from the combination of CITIOM's documented reliance and the expert opinion characterizing Gulfstream's conduct as gross negligence. CITIOM's claim of reliance is clearly stated in its Amended Statement of Claim: "CITIOM agreed to the Proposal relying on the express representations made by Gulfstream" [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]].

The allegation of gross negligence is supported by evidence that Gulfstream had the means to provide a better estimate but failed to do so. Gulfstream's introduction of "new data collection and analytical capabilities" in July 2023 is a critical fact [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3 [VERIFIED]]. The expert report highlights this failure as "blatant negligence," contrasting Gulfstream’s practice with competitors who are "demonstrably more proactive in providing realistic cost and downtime expectations." Furthermore, evidence shows that Gulfstream's parent company, General Dynamics, utilized discrepancy estimates in proposals for its subsidiary Jet Aviation, suggesting such a practice was neither impossible nor unknown within the broader corporate family.

### Contradictions or Concerns
The primary conflict is between Gulfstream’s contractual disclaimer and the tort-based theory of professional negligence. Gulfstream will argue that its proposal clearly and repeatedly stated that repair costs were excluded, and that CITIOM, a sophisticated entity, accepted these terms [Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief .pdf, p. 2 [VERIFIED]]. Gulfstream's defense expert will likely testify that omitting discrepancy costs from initial workscopes is a common industry practice [CITIOM v. Gulfstream - LB Expert Rebuttal Report (4-21-25).pdf, p. 2 [UNVERIFIED]].

The case will therefore hinge on whether Gulfstream's conduct can be elevated from ordinary negligence (which may be contractually disclaimed) to gross negligence (which cannot). The success of this argument depends heavily on the credibility of expert testimony and demonstrating that Gulfstream's failure to use its own data analytics constituted a conscious and reckless disregard of its duty to provide a professionally reasonable estimate.

### Evidence Strength Assessment
**Moderate.** The evidence supporting the core facts—the initial estimate, the final cost, the contractual disclaimer, and CITIOM's reliance—is strong and substantiated by verified documents. However, the crucial element of *gross negligence* currently relies heavily on the D. Farnham expert report, which is cited as an unverified document. While the factual predicate for the expert's opinion is sound (e.g., the existence of data analytics), the ultimate finding will depend on the weight given to this expert testimony during arbitration.

## Entities & Relationships
- **Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. ('CITIOM' or 'Claimant'):** The owner and operator of the Gulfstream G550 aircraft (SN 5174); the client in this matter.
- **Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation ('Gulfstream' or 'Respondent'):** The service provider responsible for the 192-month inspection and subsequent repairs.
- **D. Farnham:** Expert witness retained by CITIOM.
- **Patrick Stockton:** Manager of the Gulfstream Savannah Paint Shop, whose oversight of certain component work contributed to project delays and defects.

## Gaps & Limitations
- **Unverified Documents:** Many key documents are unverified, including the expert reports from both parties and the document citing Georgia law on exculpatory clauses. The authenticity and admissibility of these documents must be confirmed.
- **Absence of Full Contract:** While the summary references the proposal, the full contractual agreement between the parties, including any master service agreement, is not available. The precise wording of all limitation of liability and exculpatory clauses is essential.
- **Lack of Internal Gulfstream Communications:** There is no evidence from internal Gulfstream records detailing the process of creating the estimate, the decision-making behind not using available analytics, or internal assessments of project mismanagement as issues arose.
- **Limited Discovery:** The available documents reflect the parties' positions but lack the full record of depositions and produced documents that would substantiate or refute claims regarding industry standards and internal knowledge.

## Recommendations
1.  **Immediate Actions:**
    *   Subpoena and authenticate all key unverified documents, particularly the expert reports of D. Farnham and the legal analysis of Georgia negligence standards.
    *   Depose the Gulfstream personnel responsible for drafting the 192-month proposal for SN 5174 to establish the exact methodology used and to question the failure to incorporate available data analytics.
    *   Depose Patrick Stockton regarding the painting delays and lack of coordination to bolster claims of general project mismanagement.

2.  **Additional Investigation:**
    *   Serve requests for production seeking Gulfstream’s internal policies on estimation, records from its data analytics platform for G550 192-month inspections, and all project management reports for SN 5174.
    *   Engage with industry consultants to provide further evidence on whether it is standard practice for a premier MRO provider to omit all potential discrepancy costs, especially when possessing advanced analytical tools and prior history with the specific aircraft.

3.  **Risk Mitigation:**
    *   Prepare to vigorously defend against Gulfstream's contractual disclaimer defense by focusing legal arguments on the public policy exception for gross negligence under Georgia law.
    *   Develop a clear trial theme that Gulfstream's estimate was not merely inaccurate but was prepared with a reckless indifference to its professional obligations, evidenced by its failure to use its own advanced technology to provide a reasonably competent projection.

**INTERNAL LEGAL MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Senior Litigation Partner
**FROM:** [Your Name/Title]
**DATE:** October 26, 2023
**RE:** Assessment of Reasonableness Based on Industry Standards in *CITIOM v. Gulfstream* Arbitration

---

## **Executive Summary**

Industry standards are the primary objective benchmark for assessing the reasonableness of a party's professional conduct and performance. In the matter of *CITIOM v. Gulfstream*, expert analysis demonstrates that Gulfstream's actions, particularly its proposal development, project management, and communication, will be evaluated against established aviation maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) industry standards to determine if they were reasonable.

## **Factual Background**

In 2020, Respondent Gulfstream performed a 144-month inspection of an aircraft (the "Aircraft") owned by Claimant CITIOM. On June 2, 2023, Gulfstream presented a Customer Support Proposal for a 192-Month Inspection of the same Aircraft [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 5] [UNVERIFIED].

In July 2023, Gulfstream implemented "new data collection and analytical capabilities" designed to provide more accurate estimates for maintenance work [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3] [VERIFIED]. Despite possessing this new tool, Gulfstream did not update its June 2, 2023 proposal. Between July and August 2023, Gulfstream performed some maintenance on the Aircraft before the main proposal was formally signed [Evidence Gathered]. CITIOM, relying on Gulfstream's representations, agreed to the proposal [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3] [VERIFIED].

Significant delays ensued, and the Aircraft was ultimately returned to service in November 2024, nearly nine months after the initially estimated date [Evidence Gathered]. CITIOM commenced arbitration proceedings on May 31, 2024, and Gulfstream filed its Notice of Defense and Counterclaim on August 7, 2024 [Evidence Gathered]. Expert reports have since been prepared for both parties, with CITIOM's expert, D. Farnham, issuing his report on March 21, 2025 [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 1] [UNVERIFIED].

## **Analysis**

### **Key Findings**

*   **Finding 1:** The evaluation of Gulfstream's professional conduct hinges on a direct comparison to established industry standards. CITIOM's primary argument is that Gulfstream's performance deviated from these standards, rendering its actions unreasonable [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 4] [UNVERIFIED]. This strategy is identified as crucial for CITIOM to overcome contractual limitations on remedies and damages [In re CITCOM v Gulfstream..., p. 10] [UNVERIFIED].

*   **Finding 2:** Gulfstream’s failure to update its June 2, 2023 proposal using its new analytical capabilities, which were available from July 2023, is a central pillar of CITIOM's claim. This omission is presented as a specific failure that prevented more accurate projections and demonstrates a deviation from reasonable professional conduct and industry best practices [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3] [VERIFIED].

*   **Finding 3:** The reasonableness of Gulfstream's performance is being assessed across multiple domains, each with its own corresponding industry benchmark. These include:
    *   **Proposal Development:** Assessed against 'Industry Standards for Proposal Development' [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 2] [UNVERIFIED].
    *   **Corrosion Management:** Assessed against 'Standard Corrosion Assessment Procedures' [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 2] [UNVERIFIED].
    *   **Project Management & Communication:** Assessed via 'Comparative Analysis with Industry Standards' and 'Industry Benchmarking for MRO Services' [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 2] [UNVERIFIED].
    *   **Loss of Use Damages:** Assessed against 'Industry Standards for Loss of Use Calculations' [Evidence Gathered].

### **Supporting Evidence**

The strongest evidence supporting the use of industry standards as a metric for reasonableness comes from the structure and stated purpose of the expert report by D. Farnham, retained by CITIOM. The report explicitly outlines its intent to evaluate Gulfstream's performance against industry benchmarks [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, p. 4] [UNVERIFIED]. The report's section titles, such as "Comparative Analysis with Industry Standards," "Industry Benchmarking for MRO Services," and "Comparison to Industry Best Practices," confirm this analytical framework [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy.pdf, pp. 2, 23] [UNVERIFIED].

This expert-driven approach is substantiated by a verified source, the *CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim*, which establishes the key fact that Gulfstream possessed "new data collection and analytical capabilities" in July 2023 but failed to use them to amend its proposal [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3] [VERIFIED]. This fact directly supports the expert's conclusion that Gulfstream's proposal and planning were deficient and unreasonable when measured against its own capabilities and industry expectations.

### **Contradictions or Concerns**

Gulfstream's defense presents a significant challenge. It relies on the express terms of its proposal, which "clearly states" that the "correction of discrepancies is not included in the quoted price" [Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief .pdf, p. 2] [VERIFIED]. This contractual language will be used to argue that CITIOM's expectations for an all-inclusive estimate were unreasonable from the outset.

Furthermore, Gulfstream has retained its own expert, Leonard A. Beauchemin, who directly rebuts CITIOM's expert. Beauchemin's report asserts that the Farnham report "misstates the industry standard for information considered by, and provided to, MROs" and "misconstrues the respective roles and responsibilities of the owner/operator and the MRO" [CITIOM v. Gulfstream - LB Expert Rebuttal Report (4-21-25).pdf, p. 2] [UNVERIFIED]. This sets the stage for a "battle of the experts" on the central issue of what constitutes the applicable industry standard.

### **Evidence Strength Assessment**

**Rating: Strong**

The evidence supporting the hypothesis that industry standards are critical for assessing reasonableness is strong. This conclusion is anchored by a verified filing (*CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim*) that establishes a key factual predicate: Gulfstream's possession and non-use of advanced analytical tools. While the primary analytical documents (the expert reports) remain unverified, their consistent thematic focus, as detailed in outlines and summaries, provides a robust and coherent framework for CITIOM's case. The existence of a direct rebuttal from Gulfstream's expert does not weaken the evidence for the *relevance* of industry standards; rather, it confirms that this is the central battleground of the dispute.

## **Entities & Relationships**

*   **Claimant:** Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. (“CITIOM”), owner of the Aircraft.
*   **Respondent:** Gulfstream, the aircraft manufacturer and MRO service provider that conducted the 192-Month Inspection.
*   **Claimant's Expert (Industry Standards):** D. Farnham, authored a report assessing Gulfstream's performance against MRO industry standards.
*   **Claimant's Expert (Damages):** Michael Brown (FAZ Forensics), providing testimony on damages based on industry-standard assumptions.
*   **Respondent's Expert:** Leonard A. Beauchemin, retained by Gulfstream to rebut the expert report of D. Farnham.

## **Gaps & Limitations**

*   **Unverified Documents:** The most significant limitation is that the vast majority of the cited documents, including the expert reports from D. Farnham and L. Beauchemin, are unverified. Their contents are inferred from summaries, outlines, and briefs. The analysis is contingent on these summaries being accurate representations of the full documents.
*   **Lack of Deposition Testimony:** The record contains no deposition testimony from key personnel at Gulfstream regarding the development and intended use of the "new data collection and analytical capabilities" or the decision-making process behind the June 2, 2023 proposal.
*   **Limited Technical Detail:** Specifics regarding the "new data collection and analytical capabilities" are absent. Understanding the tool's inputs, outputs, and predictive power is essential to substantiating the claim that its use would have materially changed the proposal.

## **Recommendations**

1.  **Immediate Actions:**
    *   Prioritize obtaining and conducting a thorough review of the complete, final versions of all unverified documents, particularly the expert reports of D. Farnham and Leonard A. Beauchemin.
    *   Schedule and conduct a preparatory session with D. Farnham to stress-test his opinions against the counter-arguments raised in the Beauchemin rebuttal report.

2.  **Additional Investigation:**
    *   Serve supplemental requests for production on Gulfstream specifically targeting all internal documentation, algorithms, training materials, and reports related to its July 2023 "new data collection and analytical capabilities."
    *   Depose the Gulfstream personnel responsible for the development of the new analytical tool and the creation of the June 2, 2023 proposal to establish a timeline and rationale for not updating the estimate.

3.  **Risk Mitigation:**
    *   Prepare a detailed cross-examination outline for Gulfstream's expert, Leonard Beauchemin, focused on exposing potential weaknesses or inconsistencies in his definition and application of industry standards.
    *   Develop legal arguments that Gulfstream's failure to utilize its own superior data and knowledge to provide a reasonably accurate proposal constitutes gross negligence or a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing, sufficient to overcome the contractual disclaimer regarding "correction of discrepancies."

results.query: What is the evidentiary strength of the expert opinions?
results.hypothesis: The case involves significant disputes over expert testimony regarding aircraft maintenance, specifically concerning Gulfstream's alleged failure to identify and address corrosion issues during the 144-month inspection in 2020 and July 2023 maintenance, and/or the 192-Month Inspection, leading to subsequent exacerbation. Expert opinions, such as D. Farnham's (dated March 21, 2025), assert Gulfstream's failure, focusing on economic damages incurred due to the aircraft being out of service from January 29, 2024, through November 29, 2024. An 'LB Expert Rebuttal Report' (dated April 21, 2025) also exists, with LB being involved in a 144-month inspection and knowledgeable about industry standards like MSG-3 and MPIG. The 192-month inspection was planned for late 2024/early 2025, with AVCON approving Gulfstream's Customer Support Proposal #Q-11876 in September 2023. The evidentiary strength of such opinions will hinge on challenges to their methodology (e.g., adherence to industry standards like MSG-3, interpretation of manufacturer's manuals), factual basis (e.g., actual conditions during inspections, internal records), and qualifications. The confirmed existence of these reports and a rebuttal further underscores the central role of expert testimony and its legal and factual scrutiny within this arbitration.

**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Senior Partner
**FROM:** [Your Name]
**DATE:** October 26, 2023
**RE:** Evidentiary Strength of Expert Opinions in *Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. v. Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation*, No. G-24-115-AA

---

### **Executive Summary**

The evidentiary strength of CITIOM’s expert opinions is **Moderate**. Our technical and financial experts, D. Farnham and FAZ Forensics respectively, present a well-qualified and methodologically sound prima facie case for both liability and damages. However, the existence of a direct rebuttal from a qualified opposing expert creates a central "battle of the experts," making the outcome contingent on the tribunal’s assessment of their competing testimony regarding industry standards and responsibilities.

### **Factual Background**

This arbitration arises from alleged malfeasance by Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation ("Gulfstream") in the maintenance of a Gulfstream G550 aircraft, Serial Number 5174 (the "Aircraft"), owned by Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. (“CITIOM”) [40, VERIFIED], [27, UNVERIFIED].

In 2020, Gulfstream performed a 144-month inspection on the Aircraft [64, UNVERIFIED], [70, UNVERIFIED]. CITIOM’s expert, D. Farnham, opines that Gulfstream failed to identify and address significant corrosion issues during this and subsequent maintenance in July 2023 [34, UNVERIFIED].

In September 2023, CITIOM, through its operator AVCON, approved Gulfstream's proposal for a 192-month inspection [Working Hypothesis]. The proposal quoted a work scope cost of approximately $835,931 and an estimated downtime of 35-45 business days [42, VERIFIED], [17, UNVERIFIED]. The Aircraft was inducted for this inspection, and its time out of service commenced on January 29, 2024 [Working Hypothesis].

During the inspection, the required labor allegedly "ballooned from 2,800 to 26,000+ manhours" [82, UNVERIFIED]. This resulted in the Aircraft remaining out of service for a projected period through November 29, 2024, far exceeding the initial estimate [28, UNVERIFIED].

In support of its claims, CITIOM retained D. Farnham as a technical expert and FAZ Forensics (specifically Michael Brown) as a damages expert. Mr. Farnham produced his expert report on March 21, 2025 [46, UNVERIFIED], and FAZ produced its damages report around April 2, 2025 [3, UNVERIFIED]. In response, Gulfstream retained its own expert, who produced the "LB Expert Rebuttal Report" on April 21, 2025, directly challenging Mr. Farnham's conclusions [73, UNVERIFIED], [85, UNVERIFIED].

### **Analysis**

#### **Key Findings**

*   **CITIOM’s case is bifurcated between two well-qualified experts:** D. Farnham, an aviation maintenance professional with over 50 years of experience, provides opinions on liability, specifically Gulfstream’s technical failures [7, UNVERIFIED], [35, UNVERIFIED]. FAZ Forensics, whose principal is a CPA, CFE, and CFF with approximately 40 years of experience, provides a detailed calculation of economic damages [FAZ Forensics expert qualifications], [39, UNVERIFIED].
*   **Farnham's liability opinion is based on direct observation and extensive experience, but its core premises are directly contested.** Farnham asserts that Gulfstream provided unrealistic estimates, failed to plan for known corrosion, and exhibited poor project oversight [81, UNVERIFIED]. He bases this on direct observation at Gulfstream’s St. Louis facility and his professional expertise [36, UNVERIFIED]. However, Gulfstream's rebuttal expert (LB) directly attacks these conclusions, arguing Farnham misconstrues industry standards and the respective responsibilities of the owner/operator versus the maintenance facility [73, UNVERIFIED], [74, UNVERIFIED].
*   **The damages calculation by FAZ Forensics is methodologically robust but entirely contingent on establishing liability.** The FAZ Report calculates total damages at approximately €2.4 million, comprising €1.6M in lost profit and €814k in alternate transport costs [16, UNVERIFIED]. The methodology relies on standard forensic accounting principles, historical data from Avcon Jet, and actual invoices [Evidence Gathered]. Crucially, its "but-for" scenario, assuming an April 1, 2024, return-to-service date, is anchored to Gulfstream's own 35-45 day downtime estimate [17, UNVERIFIED]. However, the report explicitly states its conclusions are based on the assumption that Gulfstream’s liability will be established by CITIOM [19, UNVERIFIED].

#### **Supporting Evidence**

The strength of CITIOM’s expert evidence lies in its foundation and qualifications.
*   **D. Farnham (Liability):** His extensive 50-year career across major aircraft manufacturers lends significant weight to his opinions [7, UNVERIFIED]. His methodology includes not only document review but also "Direct observation and documentation of work processes" at the facility in question [2, UNVERIFIED], [36, UNVERIFIED]. His opinion that Gulfstream failed to identify corrosion during prior maintenance is a powerful claim of negligence [34, UNVERIFIED].
*   **FAZ Forensics (Damages):** The expert, Michael Brown, possesses high-level certifications (CPA, CFE, CFF) and a detailed CV [FAZ Forensics expert qualifications]. The damages model is transparent, using historical charter income data and actual invoices for costs incurred [Evidence Gathered]. The use of Gulfstream's own proposal as the baseline for the "but-for" world is a particularly strong piece of evidence that will be difficult for Gulfstream to refute without discrediting its own initial projections [17, UNVERIFIED]. The total damages are clearly broken down into lost contribution (€1,613,175) and consequential costs (€814,067) [54, UNVERIFIED], [55, UNVERIFIED].

#### **Contradictions or Concerns**

The primary weakness is the direct and fundamental conflict between the liability experts.
*   **Battle of Experts:** The "LB Expert Rebuttal Report" creates a direct clash on the dispositive issue of liability. LB contends that Farnham misstates industry standards for MRO proposals and misallocates the responsibility between the owner and the maintenance provider [73, UNVERIFIED], [74, UNVERIFIED]. #### **Evidence Strength Assessment**

**Overall Rating: Moderate**

The evidence is rated as Moderate because while CITIOM’s experts are highly credible and their reports are methodologically detailed, they do not go unrebutted. Farnham’s opinion, the lynchpin of the entire case, is directly challenged on its foundational premises by a competing expert. The damages calculation is strong on its own terms but has no independent force. The outcome of this arbitration will likely be determined by which expert’s interpretation of industry standards and professional responsibility the tribunal finds more persuasive after direct and cross-examination.

### **Gaps & Limitations**

*   **Areas for Further Investigation:** Discovery should be aimed at securing the aforementioned internal Gulfstream documents. Depositions of all three experts (Farnham, Brown, and LB) are essential to probe the bases for their opinions and their responses to contrary evidence.
*   **Limitations of Available Documents:** The vast majority of citations supporting this memorandum are from documents labeled "[UNVERIFIED]". This analysis is therefore contingent on the accuracy of the extracted information. The conclusions herein must be considered preliminary until all source documents, particularly the expert reports themselves, are obtained and authenticated.

### **Recommendations**

1.  **Immediate Actions:**
    *   Schedule a working session with Mr. Farnham and Mr. Brown to analyze the LB Rebuttal Report and prepare robust defenses for their opinions and methodologies.
    *   Develop a comprehensive cross-examination outline for Gulfstream’s expert, LB, focusing on the factual basis for his claims regarding industry standards and any potential biases.

2.  **Additional Investigation Needed:**
    *   Prioritize the verification and authentication of all cited expert reports and key evidentiary documents.
    *   Serve targeted discovery requests on Gulfstream for internal communications and project management documentation concerning both the 2020 144-month and the current 192-month inspections of the Aircraft.

3.  **Risk Mitigation Steps:**
    *   Recognize and plan for the high risk associated with a "battle of the experts" scenario. The case is not a clear-cut factual matter and depends heavily on testimonial credibility.
    *   Based on this Moderate strength assessment, consider developing a settlement strategy that leverages the well-documented damages calculation and Gulfstream's own initial flawed proposal, while accounting for the risk that we may not prevail on the core liability question.

results.hypothesis: The legal dispute centers on Gulfstream's alleged failure to adequately perform maintenance and inspection services, specifically failing to identify and address existing corrosion issues during the 144-month inspection in 2020 and during maintenance in July 2023. This untimeliness and inadequacy, which expert Danny Farnham attributes partly to 'inadequate staffing levels and inefficient workforce management practices,' directly contributed to the recurrence and exacerbation of corrosion findings during the subsequent 192-month inspection, leading to 'delays and increased costs.' This alleged deviation from mandated 'rigorous inspection protocols' and industry standards implies direct damages and legal liability for Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd., potentially amounting to approximately €2.4 million, due to economic damages such as 'loss of use of the Aircraft and other consequential costs.' The investigation will focus on the details of the 144-month inspection (2020), July 2023 maintenance, Gulfstream's workforce practices, and the causal link to the exacerbation of issues during the 192-month inspection, with technical expert Danny Farnham expected to testify on these deficiencies.
results.final_output:
**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Senior Litigation Partner
**FROM:** [Your Name/Title]
**DATE:** May 21, 2024
**CASE:** *Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. v. Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation*, No. G-24-115-AA
**SUBJECT:** Analysis of Liability Arising from the Timing of Gulfstream's Analytics

---

### **Executive Summary**
The timing of Gulfstream's analytics is central to its potential liability in this dispute. Claimant's case hinges on the fact that Gulfstream introduced "new data collection and analytical capabilities" in July 2023 but allegedly failed to utilize them when preparing the subsequent proposal for the 192-month inspection [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3]. This failure to apply available technology at a critical pre-contractual stage forms the basis for CITIOM's claims of negligent misrepresentation and fraudulent inducement, arguing that it detrimentally relied on a foreseeably inaccurate estimate for cost and downtime.

### **Factual Background**
The current dispute arises from maintenance and inspection services performed by Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation ("Gulfstream") on a G550 aircraft, Serial Number 5174, owned by Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. ("CITIOM").

In 2020, Gulfstream performed a 144-month inspection on the aircraft. During this service, Gulfstream identified and repaired internal corrosion in the horizontal stabilizer [Bassim Draft Witness Statement, p. 2]. The final cost of this inspection was approximately $1 million, nearly three times Gulfstream's initial estimate [Bassim Draft Witness Statement, p. 2].

In July 2023, Gulfstream publicly announced the introduction of "new data collection and analytical capabilities" designed to improve the accuracy of maintenance forecasts [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3; CITIOM Statement of Claim, p. 3]. Subsequent to this, Gulfstream provided CITIOM with a proposal for the aircraft's 192-month inspection. The proposal estimated the work would require 2,800 man-hours with a downtime of 35-45 business days, targeting an April 1, 2024, return-to-service date (Evidence Gathered). CITIOM states it agreed to this proposal in reliance on Gulfstream's representations and specialized knowledge [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3].

The aircraft was input for the 192-month inspection at Gulfstream's St. Louis facility on January 29, 2024 (Evidence Gathered). Shortly thereafter, Gulfstream reported the discovery of significant corrosion that "far exceeded typical findings" (Evidence Gathered) [CITIOM Statement of Claim, p. 4]. CITIOM alleges that this corrosion was in the same areas previously repaired by Gulfstream and should have been identified and addressed during prior maintenance events [Claimant CITIOM Pre-Hearing Brief - Apr 14 2025 (1), p. 3] [UNVERIFIED]; [Bassim Draft Witness Statement, p. 2].

The scope of work expanded dramatically, ultimately exceeding 27,000 man-hours, compared to a fleet average of approximately 5,400 hours for similar inspections (Evidence Gathered). The return-to-service date was repeatedly delayed, first to June 21, 2024, and the work was ultimately concluded on November 29, 2024 (Evidence Gathered). CITIOM has commenced arbitration, alleging fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation and seeking damages of approximately €2.4 million for loss of use and other consequential costs (Working Hypothesis).

### **Analysis**

#### **Key Findings**
1.  **Possession of Advanced Analytics Prior to Proposal:** Gulfstream possessed "new data collection and analytical capabilities" as of July 2023, several months before it issued the 192-month inspection proposal and CITIOM delivered the aircraft for service [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3; CITIOM Statement of Claim, p. 3]. The timing establishes that Gulfstream had the *means* to potentially provide a more accurate forecast.

2.  **Allegation of Failure to Utilize Analytics:** CITIOM directly alleges that despite having these new capabilities, Gulfstream failed to apply them, leading to a misleadingly low estimate [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3; CITIOM Statement of Claim, p. 3]. CITIOM's expert, D. Farnham, reportedly identifies "Proposal Process Deficiencies" and a failure to use "Knowledge of Aircraft History that Should Have Informed Planning" [NO exhibits - CITIOM EXPERT REPORT - D. Farnham Expert Report - Mar 21 2025 copy, p. 2] [UNVERIFIED].

3.  **Detrimental Reliance:** CITIOM claims it agreed to the proposal specifically "relying on the express representations made by Gulfstream" and its specialized knowledge [CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3]. This reliance is the causal link between Gulfstream's allegedly deficient pre-proposal analytics and CITIOM's claimed economic damages.

4.  **History of Prior Negligence:** The claim is strengthened by allegations that Gulfstream's inadequate performance during the 2020 144-month inspection and July 2023 maintenance contributed to the corrosion issues [Working Hypothesis]. A witness statement asserts that corrosion found during the 192-month inspection "should have been identified and addressed" earlier by Gulfstream [Bassim Draft Witness Statement, p. 2].

#### **Supporting Evidence**
The strongest evidence supporting CITIOM's theory of liability is derived from its own verified pleadings, which establish a critical timeline:
-   **[14], [45] CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3; CITIOM Statement of Claim, p. 3:** "In July 2023, Gulfstream introduced 'new data collection and analytical capabilities'..." This fact is the anchor for the entire claim.
-   **[15], [46] CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3; CITIOM Statement of Claim, p. 3:** "Despite Gulfstream having these capabilities since July 2023 – well before CITIOM input the Aircraft...Gulfstream failed to provide CITIOM with a realistic or accurate estimate..." This explicitly links the timing of the new technology to the alleged breach of duty.
-   **[16] CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim, p. 3:** "CITIOM agreed to the Proposal relying on the express representations made by Gulfstream..." This establishes the element of reliance necessary for a misrepresentation claim.
-   **[81] Bassim Draft Witness Statement, p. 2:** "I believe corrosion issues later found during the 192-month inspection should have been identified and addressed during the 144-month inspection..." This supports the argument that Gulfstream had, or should have had, prior knowledge of the aircraft's deteriorating condition.

Gulfstream's primary defense is also documented in verified evidence:
-   **[13] Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief, p. 2:** "The proposal that Gulfstream provided to Claimant for the 192-month inspection clearly states that the cost and downtime estimates are based solely on the tasks in the inspection package and do not include the cost or downtime associated with correcting discrepancies found during the inspection."

#### **Contradictions or Concerns**
A significant conflict exists between Gulfstream's reliance on the explicit, written exclusions in its proposal [13] and CITIOM's claim of reliance on other "express representations" [16]. The viability of CITIOM's claim will likely depend on whether it can prove fraudulent inducement, which would vitiate the contractual exclusions.

The most pressing concern is that the technical backbone of CITIOM's case, the expert report by D. Farnham, is cited but marked as [UNVERIFIED]. Without this report, allegations of "inadequate staffing," "inefficient workforce management," and specific "Proposal Process Deficiencies" are unsubstantiated hypotheses.

#### **Evidence Strength Assessment**
**Moderate.** The evidence is strong in establishing the timeline and the core allegations from CITIOM's perspective, supported by verified pleadings. Gulfstream's contractual defense is likewise clearly documented and verified. The assessment is downgraded to Moderate because the critical technical evidence from expert D. Farnham, which is necessary to prove *why* Gulfstream's estimate was deficient and how its prior maintenance failed, remains unverified.

### **Entities & Relationships**
-   **Claimant:** Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. (CITIOM) - Owner of the Gulfstream G550 aircraft.
-   **Respondent & Counter-Claimant:** Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation (Gulfstream) - The aircraft manufacturer and maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) provider.
-   **Claimant's Technical Expert:** Danny Farnham - Expected to testify regarding technical deficiencies in Gulfstream's maintenance work.
-   **Claimant's Financial Expert:** FAZ Report - Provides opinion on CITIOM's economic damages.

### **Gaps & Limitations**
-   **Unverified Foundational Documents:** The expert reports of D. Farnham (both initial and rebuttal) and the FAZ Report on economic damages are not verified. These documents are essential for substantiating the technical claims and quantifying damages.
-   **Absence of Key Records:** The investigation lacks the specific maintenance and inspection records from the 2020 144-month inspection and the July 2023 maintenance event. These are required to verify claims of prior negligence.
-   **No Data on "New Analytics":** No discovery has been produced detailing the nature of Gulfstream's "new data collection and analytical capabilities," their intended function, or any internal documents regarding their implementation or use in the proposal process.
-   **The Proposal Document:** While referenced extensively, the actual proposal document provided to CITIOM for the 192-month inspection is not included in the evidence. Its precise language is critical.

### **Recommendations**
1.  **Immediate Actions:**
    *   Prioritize obtaining and verifying all currently unverified documents, with the highest priority on the D. Farnham expert report dated March 21, 2025, and the corresponding rebuttal report.

2.  **Additional Investigation Needed:**
    *   Serve targeted Requests for Production on Gulfstream for all documents "concerning" the "new data collection and analytical capabilities" introduced in July 2023, including internal policies on their use in generating maintenance proposals.
    *   Depose Gulfstream personnel from the St. Louis facility who were responsible for preparing the 192-month inspection proposal for this specific aircraft to determine what historical data and analytical tools they used.
    *   Subpoena the complete, unredacted maintenance and invoicing records for all work performed by Gulfstream on aircraft 5174, particularly the 144-month inspection in 2020.

3.  **Risk Mitigation Steps:**
    *   Anticipate Gulfstream's defense centered on the proposal's exclusionary clause. Develop a legal strategy focused on fraudulent inducement and/or negligent misrepresentation, arguing that Gulfstream had a superior knowledge base due to its new analytics and past service history, and a duty to provide a good-faith estimate that was not recklessly misleading.
    *   Assess the strength of the "prior negligence" argument. If it can be proven that Gulfstream's own faulty repairs in 2020 led to the exacerbated corrosion, it significantly weakens their defense that the findings were unforeseeable.

**TO:** Senior Partner
**FROM:** [Your Name/Associate]
**DATE:** May 24, 2024
**RE:** CITIOM v. Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation; Analysis of Claimant's Remedies and Evidentiary Support

---

### **Executive Summary**

Claimant CITIOM is seeking approximately €2.4 million in consequential damages from Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation in a CPR arbitration proceeding. The claim, supported by a formal Statement of Claim and an expert financial report, alleges that Gulfstream's breach of warranty and mismanagement of a 192-month inspection caused a 10-month operational loss of its aircraft. While the damages are well-quantified, their recoverability is challenged by Gulfstream's contractual defense that the governing agreement explicitly excludes liability for such consequential losses.

### **Factual Background**

The dispute originates from a 192-month inspection of a Gulfstream G550 Aircraft, Serial Number 5174 (the "Aircraft"), owned by Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd. ("CITIOM"). On June 2, 2023, Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation ("Gulfstream") provided CITIOM with a customer support proposal for the inspection, quoting a cost of $835,931 and estimating a downtime of 35-45 business days, with an anticipated return-to-service date of April 1, 2024 [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3; CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3]. CITIOM alleges it accepted this proposal in reliance upon Gulfstream's express representations [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3].

The Aircraft was inducted for service on January 29, 2024. However, it remained out of service through November 29, 2024, a period of approximately 10 months [No Exhibits - CITIOM v. Gulfstream-FAZ Report copy.pdf, p. 3 [UNVERIFIED]]. CITIOM attributes this extensive delay to Gulfstream's breach of warranty, failure to perform repairs in a reasonable time, mismanagement of the inspection process, and misclassification of warranty-covered repairs as CITIOM's expense. Further, CITIOM alleges that Gulfstream failed to identify and address corrosion issues during prior maintenance events in 2020 and 2023, exacerbating the findings and work required during the 192-month inspection.

As a result, CITIOM has initiated arbitration proceedings pursuant to a dispute resolution clause in the governing agreement [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 2]. The proceedings are subject to CPR Administered Arbitration Rules and the laws of the State of Georgia [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 2; CITIOM Amended Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3]. CITIOM has submitted a Statement of Claim and retained experts to quantify its damages.

### **Analysis**

#### **Key Findings**

1.  **CITIOM Seeks €2.4 Million in Consequential Damages:** CITIOM's claim is for specific economic damages totaling approximately €2.4 million. This amount is comprised of €1,613,175 for "Lost Financial Contribution" (representing lost net profit from charter operations in 2024) and €814,067 for "Additional Consequential Costs" (representing out-of-pocket travel expenses incurred due to the Aircraft's unavailability) [CITIOM v. Gulfstream-FAZ Report.pdf, p. 2 [UNVERIFIED]].

2.  **Legal Basis for Claims:** The claims are founded on allegations of breach of warranty, failure to perform required warranty repairs within a reasonable time, and causing the warranty to fail of its essential purpose [CITIOM v. Gulfstream-FAZ Report.pdf, p. 2 [UNVERIFIED]]. CITIOM further alleges that Gulfstream's initial proposal was misleading, as it failed to account for work Gulfstream knew or should have known would be required, especially given new analytical capabilities it possessed since July 2023 [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3].

3.  **Damages are Quantified by Expert Analysis:** The damages are detailed in an expert report prepared by FAZ Forensics, retained by CITIOM's counsel. This report provides the methodology and data used to calculate the lost income and additional costs stemming from the Aircraft being out of service from January 29, 2024, through November 29, 2024 [CITIOM v. Gulfstream-FAZ Report.pdf, p. 2 [UNVERIFIED]]. A separate technical expert, D. Farnham, provides support for the underlying claims of maintenance failures [No Exhibits - CITIOM v. Gulfstream-FAZ Report copy.pdf, p. 7 [UNVERIFIED]].

4.  **Gulfstream's Defense Rests on Contractual Exclusions:** Gulfstream’s defense, articulated in its Prehearing Brief, is that its proposal explicitly excluded the costs and downtime associated with correcting discrepancies found during the inspection. The proposal allegedly states that "the 'correction of discrepancies is not included in the quoted price'" and that it "'does not include repairs to the Aircraft resulting from discrepancies . . . discovered'" during the workscope [Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief .pdf, p. 2]. An unverified document further indicates the agreement contains a broad clause excluding all consequential damages [In re CITCOM v Gulfstream - Analysis of Claims and Defenses Related to Repairs on GS550-5174(80915932.pdf, p. 3 [UNVERIFIED]].

#### **Supporting Evidence**

The strongest evidence supporting CITIOM's claim structure comes from the **CITIOM Statement of Claim** and the unverified **FAZ Forensics Report**. The Statement of Claim establishes CITIOM's reliance on the initial proposal's cost and downtime estimates [$835,931 and 35-45 business days] [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3]. The unverified FAZ Report provides a clear and itemized calculation of the €2.4 million in damages sought, linking them directly to the 10-month period the Aircraft was unavailable [CITIOM v. Gulfstream-FAZ Report.pdf, p. 2 [UNVERIFIED]].

Conversely, Gulfstream's defense is strongly supported by its **Prehearing Brief**, which contains direct quotations from the proposal stipulating that costs for correcting discrepancies are not included in the price [Gulfstream - Prehearing Brief .pdf, p. 2]. This documentary evidence directly confronts CITIOM's assertion that it was misled by the initial quote.

#### **Contradictions or Concerns**

-   **The Consequential Damages Waiver:** The most significant concern for CITIOM's case is the potential existence of a contractual clause explicitly excluding consequential damages. While this is referenced in an unverified analysis document, its confirmation in the final agreement would present a formidable, potentially fatal, barrier to recovering the €2.4 million claim for lost profits and travel costs.
-   **Factual Dispute over "New Analytical Capabilities":** CITIOM alleges Gulfstream possessed new capabilities as of July 2023 that should have led to a more accurate estimate [CITIOM Statement of Claim.pdf, p. 3]. An unverified response from Gulfstream denies this was a formal tool and frames it as a less significant process change, creating a key factual dispute over Gulfstream's good faith in its proposal [CITIOM v. Gulfstream - Gulfstream's Responses to CITIOM's Requests for Admission (2025.04.21).pdf, p. 3 [UNVERIFIED]].

#### **Evidence Strength Assessment**

**Moderate.**

The evidence is strong in establishing the timeline, the initial agreement's terms, the specific amount of damages CITIOM is seeking, and the basis for its calculations. The existence of detailed pleadings and expert reports provides a solid framework for the claim. However, the overall strength is moderated by two factors: 1) many of the key supporting documents, including the expert reports that quantify the damages and technical failures, are unverified; and 2) the potential for a contractual bar on consequential damages, which is referenced but not confirmed in a verified document, creates significant legal risk.

### **Entities & Relationships**

-   **Claimant:** CITIOM (Channel IT Isle of Man Ltd.), owner of the subject Gulfstream G550 Aircraft.
-   **Respondent:** Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation, the aircraft manufacturer and maintenance provider.
-   **Claimant's Counsel:** Watson Farley & Williams LLP.
-   **Claimant's Experts:** FAZ Forensics (financial damages); D. Farnham (technical analysis).

### **Gaps & Limitations**

-   **Evidence Not Found:** Verified copies of several critical documents are absent, including: the FAZ Forensics damage report, the D. Farnham technical expert report, and most importantly, the complete, executed Work Authorization Agreement and its Terms and Conditions which would contain the definitive language on warranties and damage limitations.
-   **Areas Needing Further Investigation:** The primary area for investigation is the precise language of the damage exclusion clause within the governing agreement. Secondly, discovery should focus on Gulfstream's internal communications regarding its "new analytical capabilities" in mid-2023 to substantiate the claim of a misleading proposal.
-   **Limitations:** This memorandum is based on available documentation, a significant portion of which is unverified. The legal analysis, particularly regarding the viability of the consequential damages claim, is preliminary and contingent upon the exact terms of the governing contract.

### **Recommendations**

1.  **Immediate Actions:**
    -   Immediately obtain and review a verified, fully executed copy of the June 2, 2023 Proposal, including all attachments and referenced Terms and Conditions. The analysis of the limitation of liability and damages exclusion clause is the highest priority.

2.  **Additional Investigation:**
    -   Conduct a thorough legal analysis under Georgia law of the enforceability of consequential damage waivers in the context of a warranty that has allegedly "failed of its essential purpose."
    -   Initiate discovery targeted at Gulfstream's internal knowledge and application of its "new data collection and analytical capabilities" prior to issuing the June 2023 proposal to CITIOM.
    -   Quantify direct damages (e.g., costs of misclassified repairs, overcharges) that would not be barred by a consequential damages waiver, as the current FAZ report explicitly excludes these.

3.  **Risk Mitigation:**
    -   Advise the client that if the agreement contains a clear and enforceable waiver of consequential damages, the likelihood of recovering the claimed €2.4 million is substantially reduced.
    -   Develop an alternative litigation strategy focused on direct damages and potentially arguing that Gulfstream’s conduct constitutes gross negligence, which can sometimes overcome contractual liability limitations under Georgia law.

CITIOM commenced this action against Respondent-Counter-Claimant Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation ('Respondent' or 'Gulfstream') for its fraudulent and negligent mishandling of its inspection and service of the Aircraft.
Gulfstream's malfeasance spanned from June 2023 misleading proposal, designation of St. Louis facility, inefficient staffing, poorly trained technicians, to broken promises on return to service date.
The Aircraft was ultimately returned to service in November 2024 (nearly nine months after the estimated return to service date).
CITIOM incurred millions in expenditures and lost millions in profit as a direct result of Gulfstream's malfeasance.
CITIOM commenced this Arbitration on May 31, 2024 pursuant to the dispute resolution provision contained in the Proposal.
Gulfstream performed the 144-month inspection of the Aircraft at its Savannah, Georgia service center in 2020.
During the 2020 144-month inspection, the horizontal stabilizer was removed, disassembled, inspected, corrosion repaired, and lower panels/skins replaced.
Gulfstream performed maintenance on the Aircraft in July-August 2023, during which leading edges of the wings were removed and refurbished, and corrosion was repaired.
Corrosion was found in the same areas (horizontal stabilizer and under leading wing edges) that were extensively repaired by Gulfstream in prior maintenance events.
Gulfstream prepared and presented the Customer Support Proposal dated 02 June 2023 (the 'Proposal') for the 192-month inspection.
The Proposal includes Part I (Workscope Description), Part II (Contingencies and Assumptions of Proposal Offer including downtime), and Part III (Payment Terms).
The Proposal states that any downtime estimates are based on Gulfstream's general understanding and are not a contractual commitment.
The Proposal includes an Addendum for Interior Refurbishment Warranty of twenty-four (24) months or twelve hundred (1200) flight hours.
CITIOM entrusted Gulfstream with its most valuable aviation asset based on a quote promising return-to-service by April 1, 2024.
The initial quote from Gulfstream was for 2,800 hours and 35-45 business days.
Gulfstream allegedly did not inform CITIOM that the quote excluded routine discrepancy work.
Gulfstream allegedly did not warn that similar inspections at its St. Louis facility had regularly taken 100-300 days.
Gulfstream allegedly did not disclose the development of a new internal tool by July 2023 to fix forecasting failures.
The aircraft was finally returned in November 2024, eight months late.
The work performed exceeded 26,000 hours.
CITIOM lost a signed aircraft sale due to the delay.
CITIOM missed nearly a year of charter income.
CITIOM incurred hundreds of thousands in out-of-pocket costs.
CITIOM's expert, Danny Farnham, was present on-site throughout the 10-month ordeal and witnessed mismanagement, labor reassignments, engineering indecision, and communication failures.
Gulfstream's rebuttal expert did not visit the facility or observe the work, basing his defense solely on internal documents and industry generalities.
The damages analysis by FAZ Forensics is conservative, excluding reputational harm, the €1 million delta on the failed sale, and misclassified warranty work.
CITIOM seeks a total award of at least €4.1 million, along with applicable interest and costs.
Lost Charter Profit (April–Nov 2024) is claimed at €1,613,175, supported by FAZ Report and Avcon Jet flight data.
Out-of-Pocket Replacement Travel Costs are claimed at €814,067, supported by verified invoices and trip records.
Loss from Failed Aircraft Sale is claimed at €1,000,000 – €1,200,000, based on the difference between May 2024 APA and Nov 2024 resale.
Denied Warranty Work / Internal Recovery Costs are estimated at €400,000+, attributed to corrosion and rework that Gulfstream should have covered.
